name: Smalltalk
title: Smalltalk (ANSI Smalltalk)
lifecycleNote: the ANSI standard has not been revised

type.text: **No static type check**: A variable has no declared type, and a message send is resolved when it executes, so a mismatch is reported at run time
**A receiver's type is a protocol, not a class**: Any object that answers a selector is acceptable, and the compiler checks no such promise
**No sum types and no generics**: An alternative is a class hierarchy or a `Symbol` and a collection holds `Object`s, so both the branch and the element type are conventions (T4, T5)
**No namespaces**: A class is entered in the one global system dictionary, so a class name collision is a system-wide event
**`nil` is an object, not an absent type**: A send to `nil` raises `MessageNotUnderstood` rather than failing a static check
**Message passing separates a request from its implementation**: A send names a selector, and the receiver chooses the method that runs

construction.text: **Global mutable state is the default**: A class variable, a class instance variable, or a `Smalltalk at:` global is reachable from every method, so construction couples to shared state
**Objects are mutable by default**: An accessor writes a field in place, and nothing in the language makes an object immutable
**Every operation is a message**: `+`, `new`, and `size` are all sends, so a call site does not distinguish an operator from a method
**The class object holds the constructor and its `initialize` hook**: `new` and `new:` are class-side methods and a subclass can override the setup that follows
**The class browser compiles into the running system**: A change is made in the live image, and the deployed artifact is the image rather than the source files
**Open classes allow a change from anywhere**: Any tool or package can add a method to `Object`, so a change has system-wide reach

memory.text: **A garbage collector reclaims memory**: Collection runs on the virtual machine's schedule, so the program cannot choose when a pause happens
**No RAII**: A resource is released by an explicit message, though `ensure:` or `ifCurtailed:` runs a release block on the way out
**No ownership model**: A reference is an untracked alias, and only the virtual machine knows when an object is unreachable
**No manual deallocation**: An object becomes garbage, and no free message exists
**`ensure:` binds a release to a protected block**: The block runs on a normal return and on a signal that unwinds through it
**Collection is invisible in the source**: An instantiation is `new`, and no deallocation is ever written

error.text: **Failures are signals and no selector describes them**: A send may raise any `Error` subclass, so the failure set is not readable from the method name
**`on:do:` installs a structured handler**: A handler is bound to a class of signal for the duration of a block, and it returns a value to the sender
**`ensure:` and `ifCurtailed:` separate the normal path from the cleanup path**: The cleanup runs however the block exits
**`MessageNotUnderstood` is a defined signal**: A send that no method implements raises it with the receiver and the selector
**`resume:`, `return:`, and `retry` state the recovery**: A handler can resume the signal, return a value, or re-run the block
**No handler is checked to exist**: The compiler does not know which signals a send raises, so the handler is written from documentation

concurrency.text: **`Process` and `Semaphore` are part of the class library**: A scheduler multiplexes processes, and a semaphore is the synchronisation primitive
**`Monitor` and `SharedQueue` are in the class library**: The common coordination patterns ship with the environment
**`Delay` suspends a process for a stated time**: The scheduler resumes it, so a timed wait is a library call rather than a system call

**Every object is reachable from every process**: The class library supplies the synchronisation primitives, and the discipline that keeps two processes apart from one shared object is the programmer's

**The classic virtual machine decides when a process runs**: Priority decides which process resumes, and the switch points belong to the interpreter, so a process at the same priority can hold the CPU through a tight loop

platform.text: **The language is standardised independently of a vendor**: ANSI INCITS 319-1998 fixes the syntax and the protocols of the standard class library
**Several independent implementations exist**: Squeak, Pharo, VisualWorks, GNU Smalltalk, and GemStone/S each run the language
**GNU Smalltalk runs a text file as an executable**: `gst file.st` needs no image, so a program can be deployed as source
**The deployment unit is a virtual-machine image**: An image carries the classes, the methods, and the live state, so a deployment couples to one virtual machine
**The image format is not standardised**: A program moves between dialects through source, not through an image file
**Portability stops at the dialect's tools**: `Monticello`, `Metacello`, and `Seaside` are dialect packages, so a portable program stays within the ANSI subset

performance.text: **Modern dialects compile the hot path**: The Cog virtual machine of Pharo and Squeak compiles a method to machine code once it becomes hot
**The virtual machine is the optimisation boundary**: The runtime optimises a method, so no source-level tuning is needed to reach the native path
**In-line caches make a polymorphic send cheap**: A send site caches the receiver's class and its method, so a repeated send costs one lookup
**Steady-state speed is below a statically compiled language**: A dynamic send is a polymorphic call site, so a numeric inner loop is slower than in Ada or C
**Warm-up precedes peak speed**: The interpreter runs a method until the runtime decides to compile it

ecosystem.text: **The ecosystem is small and centred on a few communities**: Pharo and Squeak carry most of the active library work, and commercial Smalltalk is a niche
**Pharo and Squeak are active open-source communities**: Each ships a maintained image with tools, a package manager, and libraries
**The commercial implementations are long-lived**: VisualWorks, VA Smalltalk, and GemStone/S have decades of use
**`Metacello` and `Monticello` give package management and versioning**: A package is loaded from a repository with a version map
**Seaside and Glamorous Toolkit add depth**: A continuation-based web framework and a moldable development environment are both maintained
**A library is often image- or dialect-specific**: A package loaded into one dialect usually needs adaptation for another

evolution.text: **Pharo releases on a regular cadence with a migration guide**: A release names the changes to the image and the tools
**A file-in of source is the migration unit across dialects**: A program's classes and methods load into another image
**The ANSI standard is a stable foundation**: The standardised language does not move under a program that stays within it
**Later work is dialect-specific**: Each community extends the class library and the tools on its own, so the dialects diverge
**A dialect fork is the usual form of a break**: Squeak and Pharo diverged from a shared image, so a program may target one community only
**The image carries its own history**: An old image can hold classes and methods that the source no longer describes, so a migration needs care

domain.text: **Excellent for prototyping and live systems**: The image, the class browser, and the debugger let a system be built and changed while it runs
**A strong fit for exploratory modelling**: The uniform object model and the interactive debugger support a step-by-step design
**A web application has a framework**: Seaside serves a deployed web application with continuations, and GemStone/S adds a transactional object store
**The environment is the development tool**: A refactoring browser, a debugger, and a test runner are part of the image
**Commercial product work is rare today**: A new product team usually picks another language, so precedents and hiring are scarce

learning.text: **The image-based workflow is unfamiliar and steep**: A program is edited inside a running system, and a newcomer must learn the browser, the debugger, and the image at once
**The uniform message model must be internalised**: Control flow is a message (`ifTrue:`, `whileTrue:`) and class creation is a message, which is unlike an expression-based language
**The debugger teaches by inspection**: A `MessageNotUnderstood` opens on the failing frame with the receiver and the selector in view
**The browser shows the whole system**: A method, its senders, and its implementors are reachable from one tool
**Little feedback arrives before run time**: With no static check, a mistake appears when the path executes

syntax.text: **A message send has three small forms**: Unary (`size`), binary (`+`), and keyword (`at:put:`), and all three are sends
**Blocks give inline control flow**: `[:x | x + 1]` is a closure in the same syntax as everywhere else
**Cascades group several sends to one receiver**: `a add: 1; add: 2` sends both messages to `a`
**The grammar is small**: The language is famously described in a few lines, and the class library carries the rest
**A keyword message can nest confusingly**: `a b: c d: e` parses by fixed rules, so a reader must recall them

testing.text: **A selector or type error appears only when the line runs**: With no static check, the first execution of a path is the first check of it
**`TestCase` and the SUnit runner ship with the environment**: A test class with test-prefixed methods is run by the test runner
**The debugger opens on the failing test frame**: A failure can be inspected and fixed in the running system
**`should:raise:` asserts on a signal**: A test states the error class it expects
**The test suite lives in the image with the code**: A test is a class beside the class it tests
**An unexecuted path is untested and unchecked**: A test covers the branches it runs, and a dynamic mistake in another branch waits

security.text: **The absent static typing is a security-relevant gap**: A selector error, a wrong argument, or a type confusion is detected at run time, and an unexecuted path is not checked
**Memory safety is the virtual machine's responsibility**: The machine manages references, so a buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Smalltalk source
**The standard class library exposes no address**: There is no pointer value in the language for a program to misuse
**The image persists running state to a file**: An image is a serialised object graph, so a value that should not be saved can be written into the deployed artifact
**`perform:` reaches a method by a computed selector**: A selector built from input invokes code the source does not name
**`Compiler evaluate:` compiles a string into the running system**: An untrusted string must never reach it

tradeoffs: **The image is a deliberate development model**: A running system is editable and the image is the artifact, which is the point of the environment
**Live coding is a workflow choice**: A change is compiled into the running system; the compiler is the mechanism, and the workflow is the choice
**Open classes are deliberate flexibility**: A method can be added to any class, and the global reach of that change is the price
**The absent static typing is a design choice**: No annotation is required, so the discipline is the programmer's
**Everything is an object by design**: Classes, blocks, and `nil` are objects, and the uniformity is the language's identity
**Niche adoption is an outcome**: The language predates and influenced the mainstream object-oriented languages
verdict: Smalltalk's uniform object model keeps one kind of coupling low — a send names a selector, so a caller is not bound to the receiver's implementation, and blocks, `on:do:`, and `ensure:` give structured behaviour and recovery. The core score is nevertheless in the middle band, because the language's own constructs force coupling elsewhere: no static type check, no namespaces, no module boundary, no ownership model, global mutable state by default, and open classes that let any tool change any class. The platform cost adds a small ecosystem, an image-based deployment that couples to one virtual machine, a run-time-only error model, and a steep learning curve. Main strength: live, image-based development with a best-in-class debugger, and the language's proven influence on later object-oriented languages.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.
